facts.claim: Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) built generative models of game environments and trained an agent entirely inside its world model’s “hallucinated dream”, then ran the agent in the real game.

GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024) simulates the game DOOM with a diffusion model at 20 frames per second on a single TPU; human raters were only slightly better than chance at telling its clips from the real game.

GameNGen guesses each frame from the last 64 frames and actions, a little over 3 seconds; without noise added to those frames in training, its quality fell apart after about 10 to 20 frames of its own guesses.
GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2024), guessing one frame from real past frames, came about as close to the real frame as a compressed JPEG copy at quality 20 to 30.
When Valevski et al. (2024) retrained GameNGen reading 1, 2, 4 and up to 64 past frames, the biggest gain in quality came from going from 1 frame to 2; past that, more frames added little.
In GameNGen’s tests (Valevski et al., 2024), a model fed back its own guesses drifted even while the player stood still: without noise added in training, quality fell apart after 20 to 30 steps.

Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) is a world model of 11 billion learned numbers trained on 30,000 hours of 2D platformer videos with no action labels; it learns its own small set of actions and is played frame by frame.
Meta’s Movie Gen (October 2024) is a model of 30 billion learned numbers that makes 1080p video, 16 seconds at 16 frames a second, reading up to 73,000 video tokens at once.
OpenAI’s Sora report (February 2024) says its largest model makes up to a minute of high-fidelity video, treats video as patches across space and time, and leaves out model details.
A 1080p HD frame is 1,920 pixels across and 1,080 down.

Janner et al. (2019) trained agents partly inside a learned model, in short runs each started from real data; they needed less real data than earlier ways of using a model and learned as well as agents trained on real data alone.
